title: How many?
goal: Counting to a hundred, telling apart three different sets of numbers, counting people, and saying your age.
bekal: use numbers for counting, for things and for people — three different sets
know that numbers 2–6 bring séimhiú and 7–10 bring urú
ask *Cé mhéad …?* and give your age with *… bliain d'aois*

dialogs.title: Comhrá — Ag ullmhú don dinnéar
dialogs.intro: Late afternoon in the kitchen. Máire is getting dinner ready for guests, and Budi helps count the chairs.

lines.speaker: Máire:
lines.text: A Bhudi, an bhfuil tú saor tráthnóna?
lines.id: Budi, are you free this evening?
lines.literal: O Budi, Q is you free evening?

lines.speaker: Máire:
lines.text: Tá dinnéar mór againn. Tá seachtar ag teacht.
lines.id: We're having a big dinner. Seven people are coming.
lines.literal: is dinner big at-us. is seven-people at coming.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Seachtar! Cé mhéad cathaoir atá againn?
lines.id: Seven! How many chairs have we got?

lines.speaker: Máire:
lines.text: Tá sé chathaoir sa chistin agus trí chathaoir sa seomra suí.
lines.id: There are six chairs in the kitchen and three chairs in the sitting room.
lines.literal: is six chair in-the kitchen and three chair in-the room sitting.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Naoi gcathaoir ar fad. Tá sin go leor.
lines.literal: nine chair on length. is that enough.

lines.speaker: Máire:
lines.text: Agus tá dhá bhord againn — bord mór agus bord beag.
lines.id: And we have two tables — a big table and a small table.
lines.literal: and is two table at-us — table big and table small.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Cé mhéad duine atá sa teaghlach?
lines.id: How many people are in the family?

lines.speaker: Máire:
lines.text: Ceathrar: mise, Seán, agus beirt iníonacha.
lines.id: Four: me, Seán and two daughters.
lines.literal: four-people: me, Seán, and two-people daughters.

lines.speaker: Máire:
lines.text: Tá Sinéad sé bliana déag d'aois agus tá Órla deich mbliana d'aois.
lines.id: Sinéad is sixteen and Órla is ten.
lines.literal: is Sinéad six year teen of-age and is Órla ten year of-age.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tá mé fiche bliain d'aois. Tá mé níos sine ná iad!
lines.id: I'm twenty. I'm older than them!
lines.literal: is I twenty year of-age. is I more old than them!

notes: **Three sets of numbers, and you need to know which goes where.** For counting with no noun — phone numbers, house numbers, counting one-two-three — you use the forms with *a*: *a haon, a dó, a trí*. For things you use the bare forms: *dhá bhord, trí chathaoir*. For people there's a completely different set: *beirt, triúr, ceathrar*. Using the wrong set is no small slip — *trí* and *triúr* are as different as "three" and "a trio".

**Sé chathaoir but naoi gcathaoir.** Numbers 2 to 6 bring **séimhiú**: *dhá bhord*, *trí chathaoir*, *ceithre chathaoir*, *cúig bhord*, *sé chathaoir*. Numbers 7 to 10 bring **urú**: *seacht mbord*, *ocht gcathaoir*, *naoi gcathaoir*, *deich mbord*. The number 1 and numbers above 10 change nothing.

**The noun stays singular.** *Naoi gcathaoir*, not *naoi gcathaoireacha* — literally "nine chair". English uses a plural after numbers, so this takes a moment to get used to; think of "ten-pound note" or "a six-foot man". The only exceptions are a handful of words with special counting forms, like *bliain*, which becomes *bliana* after 3 to 10.

**Beirt iníonacha, ceathrar — people have their own set.** These ten words (*duine amháin, beirt, triúr, ceathrar, cúigear, seisear, seachtar, ochtar, naonúr, deichniúr*) are used only for human beings, and each one already contains the meaning "people". So *Tá seachtar ag teacht* is complete without the word *duine* — literally "a seven are coming".

blocks.text: Read this table from left to right, one number per row. The second column is for bare counting, the third for things, the fourth for people.

Notice three things in the "for things" column: 2 uses the form *dhá* (not *dó*), 4 uses *ceithre* (not *ceathair*), and 1 goes **after** the noun as *amháin*. All three are exceptions to learn by heart.

blocks.title: Why there's an a and an h before the numbers
items: The *a* before counting numbers is an empty marker showing that the number stands alone, with no noun. It's said very lightly, like the *a* in "about".
*A haon* and *a hocht* get an **h** because both start with a vowel — the same pattern as *go hiontach* in Unit 2. Likewise *a haon déag* and *a hocht déag*.
For phone numbers and house numbers, always use this set: *a náid* (zero), *a haon*, *a dó* … The number 087 is read *a náid, a hocht, a seacht*.

sections.title: Counting people, and saying your age

blocks.text: The ten words for counting people already contain the meaning "people", so each can stand alone as a full answer.

head: Sentence
Literally
English
rows: There are two women in the shop.
There are six children in the class.

blocks.text: *Beirt* — and only *beirt* — lenites the next word: *beirt fhear*, *beirt bhan*, *beirt mhac*. The other people-counters change nothing.

head: Gaeilge
Say it
English
rows: Tá sé sé bliana déag d'aois.

blocks.title: Bliain, bliana, mbliana — one word, three shapes
items: After 1 and 2, and after numbers above 20: **bliain**. *Bliain amháin*, *dhá bhliain*, *fiche bliain*, *tríocha bliain*.
After 3 to 6: **bliana**. *Trí bliana*, *ceithre bliana*, *cúig bliana*, *sé bliana*.
After 7 to 10: **mbliana**. *Seacht mbliana*, *ocht mbliana*, *naoi mbliana*, *deich mbliana*. The *m* in front is ordinary urú, and the *b* after it goes silent.
*D'aois* literally means "of age" and always goes on the end. Without it, *Tá mé fiche bliain* means "I've been (here) for twenty years".

sections.title: Cé mhéad — asking how many and how much

blocks.text: *Cé mhéad* is pronounced kyay VAYD, literally "what amount". The noun after it is always **singular**.

head: Gaeilge
Say it
English
rows: How many times? / How many hours?
Cé mhéad atá ar an gcaife?
kyay vayd uh-TAW er an GAH-fuh

blocks.text: Notice that even a price sits **on** the item: *Tá trí euro air* literally means "there are three euro on it". You've already seen the same *ar* pattern in *Tá ocras orm* in Unit 2, and it comes back in Unit 8.

blocks.title: Numbers you'll use every day
items: **Phone numbers** are read digit by digit using the counting set: 086 231 4457 → *a náid, a hocht, a sé — a dó, a trí, a haon — a ceathair, a ceathair, a cúig, a seacht*.
**Prices** use euro and *cent*: *dhá euro caoga* (€2.50), *seacht euro* (€7).
**Compound numbers above twenty** are built with *a*: *fiche a haon* (21), *tríocha a cúig* (35), *céad a deich* (110). The older form with *is* — *aon is fiche* — is still heard in songs and poems.

exercises.prompt: Write the numbers in counting form (with *a*).
Put the number and noun together. Remember séimhiú for 2–6 and urú for 7–10.
Fill in the right word for counting people (beirt, triúr, ceathrar, cúigear, seisear, seachtar).
